name: Casein protein

lead: Casein is taken before bed to supply amino acids slowly overnight, supporting recovery and muscle gain over time. It is the main protein in milk, making up roughly 80 percent of cow's milk protein.

In the stomach casein forms a gel and releases amino acids over several hours, while whey is absorbed faster. Its digestion profile is well documented. Published human work on casein as a muscle supplement consists largely of small exercise trials, including a registered 2025 trial that compared pre-sleep and post-exercise casein in 24 participants; the added visible muscle versus other protein has not been studied.

paras: It is sold as a powder, usually micellar casein or calcium caseinate, mixed into a shake or pudding and taken in the evening. Lifters often pair it with whey after training and use it at other times when long gaps between meals are expected.
It is a food-grade protein, not a drug. People with milk-protein allergy or intolerance avoid it; casein is a common food allergen in a small share of children.

angle.text: Users take casein before bed so amino acids reach muscle slowly overnight, supporting more muscle over time. Its slow digestion is well documented; the extra visible muscle compared with other protein has not been studied.

lead: Casein is the main protein family in milk, making up roughly 80% of cow's milk protein, and is sold as a powdered supplement (commonly micellar casein or calcium caseinate) in the bodybuilding and fitness market [1][2]. In looksmaxxing communities it is used mainly as a slow-digesting protein taken before bed, to support muscle mass and through it a fuller, more muscular physique.

The reasoning is that casein forms a gel in the stomach and releases amino acids gradually over several hours, in contrast to whey, which is absorbed faster [1][2]. Practitioners therefore pair whey around training with casein at other times, particularly overnight, so that muscle has a steady amino acid supply while they sleep [3].

Published human work on casein as a muscle supplement is mostly small exercise trials. A 2023 randomised trial in 36 young men found that protein taken before sleep after evening exercise raised overnight muscle protein synthesis, with casein and whey producing similar increases [4]. A 2025 trial in 24 soccer players compared casein taken before sleep and after training [5][6]. Casein is a food allergen for a small share of children, and people with milk-protein allergy or intolerance avoid it [1].
infobox: Forms a gel in the stomach; slow amino acid release [1]
Pre-sleep protein, meal replacement shakes, protein bars
Paint, glue, plastics, fibres, food emulsifiers [1]

paras: Casein is a group of related phosphoproteins (alpha-S1, alpha-S2, beta and kappa types) that makes up about 80% of the protein in cow's milk and a smaller share (about 20 to 60%) in human milk [1]. In milk it exists as spherical colloidal particles called micelles held together by calcium and hydrophobic interactions [1][2]. Casein precipitates at about pH 4.6, which is why it curdles in an acidic stomach and in cheesemaking [1][2].

Commercial forms include sodium and calcium caseinates, used widely as food emulsifiers and stabilisers, hydrolysed casein, in which enzymes have partly broken the protein down, and micellar casein, which keeps the natural micelle structure and is the form usually sold in sports tubs [1]. Micellar casein concentrate is produced from skim milk by microfiltration, which separates the casein micelles from whey proteins [7][8].

Casein was one of the first proteins to be described chemically, and its curd-forming behaviour has been exploited for centuries in cheesemaking [1][2]. Long before it was a sports supplement it was an industrial material: casein paint has been used as a tempera since ancient Egypt and stayed popular with commercial illustrators until acrylics displaced it in the late 1960s, casein glues were used in woodworking and in the construction of the de Havilland Albatross airliner in 1939, and casein plastics such as galalith were made into buttons [1]. The Italian fibre Lanital, invented in 1935, was spun from milk casein and sold in the United States as Aralac [1].

On the nutrition side, Mead Johnson introduced Casec in the early 1920s as a casein-based product for children with digestive problems [1]. Sodium caseinate became the most common processed form and is widely used in foods as an emulsifier [1]. Protein supplements for athletes grew mainly around dairy by-products: whey, the other milk protein, was developed into protein concentrates from the late 1960s, with a 65 percent protein concentrate produced in 1970, and it gained commercial importance in sports nutrition by the late 1980s [9]. Micellar casein, produced by microfiltering skim milk, later became the main casein form sold in tubs to lifters [7][8]. Since the early 1990s, animal-free casein has also been made by precision fermentation [1].

In the stomach casein clots into a gel that releases amino acids into the blood slowly, sometimes over several hours [1]. Hydrolysed casein is digested faster than intact casein [1]. Casein supplies essential amino acids along with calcium and phosphorus [1][2]. Reference texts describe it as a high-quality protein with a high leucine content [2]. A review comparing protein sources for athletes discusses casein alongside whey, soy and egg in terms of digestibility and amino acid content [10].

Not all casein forms clot alike. In a randomised crossover study with an in vitro digestion arm, sodium caseinate, made of small aggregates, delivered amino acids to the blood faster than micellar casein or calcium caseinate, which the authors attributed to differences in clotting in the stomach [11]. A 2025 trial in healthy volunteers compared the absorption of micellar casein with a glycomacropeptide product and free amino acids [12].

Cow's milk protein is about 80 percent casein and 20 percent whey, while human milk is closer to 60 percent whey and 40 percent casein [1][9]. Casein clots in the stomach and releases amino acids slowly, and supplement marketing and forum posts therefore describe whey as the fast protein and casein as the slow one [1][9].

Whey is the protein most associated with muscle growth and recovery after training, and a 2010 European Food Safety Authority opinion described whey as about as effective as other protein sources for strength and lean body mass [9]. The ISSN position stands say that total daily protein and its distribution matter and that both fast and slow proteins stimulate muscle protein synthesis [13][3]. A 2004 review of protein types for athletes compares casein, whey, soy and egg for digestibility and amino acid content [10]. Caseins are the major milk allergens, while whey proteins cause some milk allergies as well [9].

Users describe casein as a pre-sleep protein intended to supply amino acids overnight and limit muscle protein breakdown, usually alongside whey after training. One looksmax.org thread argues for taking casein roughly 80% of the time and whey around workouts, and adds the claim that dairy raises IGF-1. Another thread lists whey after training, casein before sleep and calcium caseinate as the cheaper everyday option, and notes the latter is calcium-based [14].

Some users say casein is harder to drink than whey because of its thick texture, and others ask about vegan powders as cheaper alternatives. On T Nation, a thread titled around casein versus whey at night asks whether the pre-bed casein is much more beneficial than a whey isolate the poster already uses [15]. Another T Nation post cites research on pre-bed protein and describes lifters who took a casein blend before bed gaining about 4 pounds more muscle over 12 weeks than controls [16]. A different member writes that he once thought a casein shake was needed immediately before bed but later changed his view on night-time nutrition [17].
Casein is also used for fullness. T Nation members describe casein as satiating and mention it as a late-night shake or as part of high-protein diets [18].

Cow's milk protein allergy affects an estimated 0.25 to 4.9% of young children, with limited data for adults; heat-treated casein may be more allergenic [1]. Casein-containing products are unsuitable for people with milk-protein allergy [1]. T Nation users also report digestive trouble with milk proteins, and one post notes that lactose-free milk still contains whey and casein, so people who react to the protein rather than the sugar are not helped by it [19][20]. Casein and gluten-free diets sometimes used for autistic children have weak supporting evidence for behavioural benefit [1].

A separate debate concerns A1 versus A2 beta-casein variants; a 2005 independent review and a 2009 European Food Safety Authority review found no identifiable link between A1 milk and chronic disease [1]. Sublingual casein-containing allergenic extracts appear on US drug labels as an allergy product and carry warnings about use in pregnancy and for children; this is a different product from food-grade casein powder [21].

The A1 and A2 variants of beta-casein differ by a single amino acid, and New Zealand researchers in the early 1990s linked A1 milk to chronic disease in observational and animal studies; an A2 milk company was later founded to market milk without the A1 form [1]. Digestion of A1 beta-casein can release a peptide called beta-casomorphin-7, which features in some of these claims, and the 2005 review and EFSA's 2009 opinion found no identifiable link to disease [1].

The International Society of Sports Nutrition position stands on protein and on nutrient timing describe protein intake of about 1.4 to 2.0 g per kg of body weight per day as sufficient for most exercising people to build muscle, and note that protein ingested before or after resistance exercise stimulates muscle protein synthesis [13][3]. They are the framework in which casein supplements are usually discussed.

A 2023 randomised controlled trial in Sports Medicine gave 36 healthy young men an evening exercise session followed by 45 g of casein, 45 g of whey or a placebo about 30 minutes before sleep. Both proteins raised overnight mitochondrial and myofibrillar protein synthesis compared with placebo, and casein and whey were similar to each other [4].

A 2025 randomised trial in Nutrients enrolled 24 male soccer players in three groups of eight: casein after training, casein before sleep, and control. After a resistance session and 30 g of micellar casein, both casein groups improved on different anaerobic performance measures (jump height and sprint mean power for pre-sleep; sprint power and fatigue index for post-exercise) compared with controls, and the two timings did not differ significantly [5][6].

A 2019 randomised trial reported that protein supplementation did not augment adaptations to endurance training [22]. Registered trials have also examined casein with leucine in people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease [23][24], casein compared with a whey-based supplement with exercise in 99 older adults [25], hydrolysed casein and appetite or energy expenditure in 33 volunteers [26], and casein glycomacropeptide in 24 healthy volunteers [27]. Most studied populations are athletes, older adults or patients rather than people seeking aesthetic changes, and no study has tested casein for facial or bone-structure appearance.

Casein is sold as micellar casein tubs, calcium caseinate and casein-whey blends by many sports nutrition brands, often marketed as a night-time protein [14]. It is also a common ingredient in protein bars, shakes and cheese, and casein derivatives serve as food emulsifiers [1]. Cottage cheese and quark, which are high in casein, are discussed in fitness forums as whole-food equivalents [28]. One T Nation thread describes a home process for extracting casein from milk and making a hydrolysate, illustrating the do-it-yourself end of the culture [29].

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums, casein sits in the wider conversation about getting enough protein cheaply while managing digestion, cost and taste: posters compare casein tubs with whey, caseinate, quark and cottage cheese, and ask which gives the thickest, most filling shake [14][28]. Because the end goal described in those threads is a leaner, more muscular body, casein is usually grouped with other body-composition tools such as lifting programmes, calorie targets and sleep rather than with anything aimed at the face [14].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org casein appears in muscle-building threads as the 'slow' counterpart to whey, with posters recommending it before bed [14]. T Nation members debate the same point with more mixed views [15][17].

timeline.event: Casein-based paint is used as a tempera medium [1].
Mead Johnson introduces Casec, a casein-based product for children with digestive problems [1].
Lanital, a fibre spun from milk casein, is invented in Italy and later sold in the US as Aralac [1].
Casein glue is used in building the de Havilland Albatross airliner [1].
A 65 percent protein whey concentrate is produced in New Zealand, an early step toward modern milk-protein supplements [9].
New Zealand researchers raise the A1 beta-casein hypothesis; animal-free casein production by fermentation begins [1].
An independent review and then EFSA find no identifiable link between A1 milk and chronic disease [1].
The International Society of Sports Nutrition publishes position stands on protein and on nutrient timing [13][3].
A randomised trial reports that pre-sleep casein or whey raises overnight muscle protein synthesis after evening exercise [4].
A trial compares pre-sleep and post-exercise casein in soccer players [5].
